en: The Book of Women (*Strīparvan*)
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Victory! (Jayam).
Gāndhārī and King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, their minds deeply agitated, went forth as if filled with longing to behold their slain sons. (Bhājana 12.2)
Then the Blessed One, the son of Parāśara, approached and beheld those two lamenting there and casting their bodies upon the ground.
Overcome with compassion, he spoke to the lord of men, who was wretched, fallen upon the ground, and whose sons had been slain, together with Vidura and Kṛṣṇa.
The non-existence of embodied beings exists constantly both before and after; toward those intermediate modifications, who would you think fit to feel attachment?
In this shoreless ocean of existence,
all living beings arise and pass away through the power of karma, like bubbles upon the water.
It is true that Suyodhana was born for the purpose of relieving the earth's burden;
having accomplished that, he has departed. Who are you to him, and who is he to you?
"O Lord of Men, do not grieve while this great assembly is underway;
not even a single spark from those who have departed returns against them."
This exertion leads only to weariness and arises from grief and calamity;
now let this affection, which is the root of the trees of suffering, be restrained.
Homage to Kāla, who exists as an unknown entity encompassed by death,
and by whom the bodies of embodied beings naturally undergo old age.
"Your sons were devoured by Time due to their own transgressions;
therefore, you ought not to be angry with the sons of Pāṇḍu for this misfortune."
The Pāṇḍavas, whose intellects are fixed on the eternal Dharma, have been wronged by you through unrighteousness; remembering their brother, do not harbor malice toward them.
Speak to Gāndhārī so that she does not suddenly sink into delusion;
for she herself previously said that righteousness is the foundation of victory.
Thus, at their word, the sons of Pṛthā, with their necks bowed low in shame, quickly approached the lord of the Kauravas, who was in a state of delusion.
Then the King, whose eye was wisdom, embraced Yudhiṣṭhira;
afterwards, he embraced Bhīma, who was composed of illusion and had been magnified by Kṛṣṇa’s intelligence.
The son of the Wind approached out of anger and was crushed by him with his two arms;
he went away in pieces, and everyone was filled with wonder.
Then the son of Dharma bowed down before his aged,
devoted wife Gāndhārī, who, out of fidelity to her husband, always kept her eyes covered with a cloth.
Having fallen down at her feet, Dharmanandana,
consumed by the fire of his wrathful gaze, burned the pair of her big toes.
Then Gāndhārī, distressed by grief for those slain and anxious for her daughters-in-law, went toward the midst of the battlefield along with the beloved wives of the kings.
Having lamented piteously there, the daughter of Subala, overwhelmed and weeping,
that devoted wife with divine vision spoke to Keśava.
"Behold these sons of mine, O Kṛṣṇa, slain in battle by Sīmantinī—those whom, when seen previously, neither the sun nor the moon had ever beheld. (Bhājana 12.21)
Behold my brave son, surrounded by the women of the inner apartments as if by apsarases,
slain before my very eyes with his thighs broken.
Behold this wife of Suyodhana, who, seeing the earth as if it were her rival— upon which the elephants have been slain and the horses have been killed— has fallen into a swoon.
Having regained consciousness, this queen of the king of kings slowly wiped away the dust for a long time and questioned her beloved.
O Lord of the Earth, how is it that you sleep with your arms embracing the earth, as if holding me in your lap while I am clad in jeweled garments, and with your mace?
O Lord of Men, how is it that Śivā, who was once wrapped in a golden couch as her bed of luxury, now sleeps here, drunk with blood? (Bhājana 12.26)
Here lies your beloved and charming younger brother, Duḥśāsana;
his blood has been drunk by Bhīma as if by a rākṣasa.
"O Lord, this beloved son of yours, Lakṣmaṇa, has been slain by the enemy;
yet he seems to desire to say something to you as if he were still alive."
The two straight gate-arches of the city of the God of Love, fallen like ivory pillars,
seem to be regarded as the tusks of the elephant of Time.
"This crown, which was fitting for you and long rested comfortably upon your head, has now fallen away here;
though once radiant, it is touched by the loss of its luster."
As you traverse the battlefield with feet drenched in blood,
the luster of the crest-jewels of kings seems to have been constantly drunk and then vomited forth.
When you, the guardian of the world, have departed for heaven out of curiosity for the Nandana grove,
fame alone remains following in your wake, as if it were the sole possessor of the pride of being blessed.
On whose other arm— adorned with radiant jewel-bangles and white as camphor—
could the earth find the bliss of resting upon Śeṣa?
That king who was once fanned with yak-tail whisks adorned with tinkling ornaments is even now being fanned by the wind from the mouths of carnivorous birds.
Thus, seeing the Kuru women dragging away Duryodhana’s wife as she cried out and writhing on the ground where she had fallen, [the people] looked on. (Bhājana 12.35)
From here, Subhadrā, out of affection for her son, is stroking her son Saubhadra,
who is covered in dust, as if she were about to offer him her breasts.
Placing her husband’s moon-like face upon her lap, Uttarā washed it with streams of tears and questioned him.
O Lord, having spoken such tender words of affection,
why do you now lie upon the ground embracing the earth, having abandoned me, your beloved?
The son of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, the offspring of the sister of the Discus-bearer,
you who were equal to Śakra in valor— how is it that you alone have been slain by the enemies?
"Surely some fortunate being among the women of heaven shall drink from this lovely face of yours, which resembles a lotus yet surpasses the lotus, as it smiles."
O beloved, he who was previously called "Anaṅga" (the bodiless one) because he lacked a body, and thus could not serve as a point of comparison for you,
has today been made meaningful by you through the destruction of his limbs.
I suspect that as you ascend to the third heaven, the row of stars, out of fear of the moon,
creates the illusion of a pearl necklace around your neck.
I, who was previously requested by you to converse as a newlywed bride—
how is it that you do not respond to me as I am speaking to you myself?
Where indeed has that courtesy of yours gone, you who are worthy of being counted among those possessing the full range of virtues,
since you now neglect me while attached to the maidens of heaven?
Since it is impossible once again to describe the excellence of the King’s fortune,
fie on those heavens whose eyes have been scorched by gazing upon your body!
Since you were equal to the Flower-Armed One (Kusumāyudha), it is certain that you truly possessed the nature of the Flower-Armed One;
otherwise, how could heroes have endured you in battle?
"Thus lamenting, these daughters-in-law of Virāṭa forcibly drag their young daughter away and go weeping toward her husband."
King Virāṭa, along with his younger brothers, his sons, and his ministers, was slain;
surrounded by his daughters-in-law, he lay upon the earth like a host of apsarases in heaven.
Seeing her husband’s face severed by Droṇa’s arrow, Sudakṣiṇā cried out loudly; she was held back by fainting, as if by a female friend.
Behold Karṇa, whose limbs have been torn apart by carnivorous beasts; the women of his household embrace him again and again and mourn him, the ultimate refuge of the Kauravas.
When his name was proclaimed, even your enemies could not find sleep; yet today you lie slain—fie on the inexhaustible cruelty of Time!
How was Karṇa— who was true to his promise and for whom the enemy of Jambha (Indra) became a petitioner for armor and earrings— reduced by the sky-goers (gods) to nothing but his ears?
The creation of the Destroyer of all things was by nature a failure;
for, having made [the world] equal to Śakra, he did not make it a witness to the kalpa.
Thus the wives of Karṇa, their ornaments disarrayed and wailing,
tear at the expanse of their breasts— the mothers of Vṛṣasena.
Behold my son-in-law Jayadratha, O Kṛṣṇa, slain;
my young daughter grieves, yet she does not know how to grieve. (Bhājana-mālā 12.55)
This Śalya, whose prowess was like a thorn to his enemies, has been slain in battle;
now that he has become a mere thorn himself, behold the women of the inner apartments.
Behold, the tongue of this King of Madra is being pulled out by crows—
by that very tongue through which he brought about the destruction of the son of Rādhā’s splendor in battle.
Behold, in battle, how Drona’s funeral rites are being performed by the brahmins, like those for a fire whose flames have been extinguished, after they have driven away the unconscious worms.
This hero Bhūriśravas, the son of Somadatta, has been slain;
the hero whose arm was severed by Kirīṭin is now being mourned by his queen.
I believe that when your arm, which serves as a sacrificial post for the battle-sacrifice and bears the banner of the sacrificial stake, was severed by Arjuna, your own fame was likewise cut away.
O Lord, as the serpent-king who bears the burden of the earth— Śeṣa, whose hand is Lakṣmī—
is drawn away by Śiva, the row of bracelets on your arm seems to cry out.
In the past, this very arm— adorned with grace— embraced those women who were adorned with love for you in the palace that was adorned with moonlight.

O Hero, when this arm of yours— which was a wish-granting tree for those in need— has been severed, what other man shall attain the status of preceptor for the initiation of widowhood among the wives of your enemies?
Who indeed, among those with gazelle-like eyes, would forcefully seize the throbbing sprout of the beauty of Keyūraka’s armlet and make it an ear-ornament? 12.64.
Thus, lamenting and overwhelmed, she spoke to the Lord of Kamala,
the most excellent Bhūriśravas, who possessed vast fame, identifying him with her own self.
Behold, the parrot who hated beneficial advice is being devoured by jackals,
like a wealthy man of inauspicious conduct by courtesans.
The earth was swiftly devastated by these low-born men with arrows that pierce to the ear;
previously, it was devastated here by dice and there by arrows by the Diademed One (Arjuna).
These beloved wives of Sudakṣiṇa, the king of Kamboja,
tear at his heart with their lamentations as if they were piercing stone itself.
These delicate women weep over Prince Bṛhadbala, who was pierced by the arrows of Saubhadra, as they gaze upon the moonlight.
These sons of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, adorned with blazing golden garlands,
lie here slain by Droṇa, shining like fallen Vidyādharas.
The Kekayas, Dhṛṣṭaketu, Jayatsena of Magadha,
and King Drupada, aged and accompanied by his ministers, sons, and kinsmen.
Alāyudha, Alambuṣa, Bhagadatta, Śrutāyudha,
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, Jalasaṃdha, and Sulocana.
Other eminent kings and thousands of heroes have been slain;
yet, surrounded by their beloved wives, they appear as if they have regained their lives.
O Kṛṣṇa, although you were capable, you disregarded them either out of desire,
or because of the destruction of all [beings], or out of hatred, or even as a sport, despite being omniscient.
When the twenty-sixth year arrives, during a mutual conflict among the Vṛṣṇis,
there will likewise follow a vast destruction of kinsmen.
"Even for you, some cause for death will arise that is likewise improper," having said this,
the daughter of Subala wept with piteous cries.

Kṛṣṇa, for whom creation, dissolution, and emergence proceed according to his own will, said to her with a smile: "This was previously ordained by Brahmā; what you have spoken is merely a repetition."
"Do not grieve in vain over this inevitable destruction;
for it was surely destined that I would slay the enemies, even though they were born of Kṣatriya lineage."
When the descendant of Daśārha had spoken thus, Dhṛtarāṣṭra questioned Yudhiṣṭhira regarding the destination of the heroes and their number at the time of destruction.
To her, Dharmarāja spoke these sweet words in the midst of battle:
"There are twenty thousand, six crores, and six [more]."
In this battle, those heroes worthy of being counted who were slain without fighting joyfully have gone to the city of the Gandharvas.
Those who turned their backs out of fear attained the state of yakṣas; however, those who remained steadfast in undiminished courage took refuge in the world of Brahmā.
Those who were slain by their mounts have now gone to the side of Mount Meru on foot;
through the grace of the sage Lomaśa, I behold this with my divine vision.
Having spoken thus, the Son of Dharma immediately ordered the performance of funeral rites for the slain kings and their kinsmen, in accordance with their respective wealth and status.
The charioteers headed by Indrasena, as well as Sañjaya, Vidura,
and Yuyutsu, went with his voice to perform the final rites for him.
Adorned with garlands, garments, and ornaments, those great chariot-warriors were placed upon the funeral pyres; as they entered them, they seemed to enter their own valor.
Then there arose from the women gathered here and there,
their necks locked with one another, a piteous sound of weeping.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, accompanied by Dhṛtarāṣṭra and his followers,
and followed by the wives of the king, went to bathe in the river.
Having been informed by his mother of the events concerning Karṇa and their secret origin,
he, out of grief, offered to his brother a handful of water mixed with tears.
Having performed for his kinsmen the rites appropriate to them according to tradition,
the king ordered tents and pavilions for the funeral ceremonies of the royal women.

Then those queens of the king, with straight and long eyes whose tears surpassed the brilliance of pearl necklaces with the cascades of their water, went to the Bhāgīrathī; their broad hips and thighs were like sandy banks, resounding with girdles as charming as *kalahaṃsa* ducks.
Thus ends the Strīparvan in the Bhāratamañjarī composed by Kṣemendra.
